title: Evening Blitz: KV-batch Handoff Handbook
content:
Purpose
This is a compact, operational handbook from tonight's evening blitz focused on reducing tail latency during sudden microbursts and stabilizing the KV-batching path across two kernels. The goal is a single-page capture of decisions, temporary mitigations, and next-day action items for handoff to daytime owners.

Context and motivation
- Several customers saw 95th->99th percentile latency drift during a 3-minute burst at 21:14 UTC on 2029-06-18. The spike correlated with a mix of short-chat and long-completion requests (seq len distribution shifted).
- Hypothesis: interaction between the new microkernel shim and KV-prefill coalescer causes a small cohort of requests to be delayed by an extra batching tick when slot reclamation and soft-eviction collide.
- Tonight's blitz was intended to: 1) reproduce locally in a reduced sandbox, 2) try targeted mitigations with minimal service impact, 3) mark changes for a controlled rollout if effective.

Participants
- Asha (lead ops, triage)
- Liam (kernel engineer, scheduler + affinity)
- Chen (profiling + perf regression author)
- Riley (oncall, rollback guard)
- Diego (kv-cache heuristics)

Timeline and what we did
- 21:00 - quick intake: pulled traces from the burst window, noted ~1200 requests that experienced an extra 15-45ms wait before kernel enqueue.
- 21:10 - replayed a subset in local sandbox using the real tokenizer distributions; reproduced the extra wait consistently when cohort sampler hit two adjacent eviction cycles.
- 21:25 - enabled microkernel shim logging to capture slot acquisition/soft-eviction sequence and confirmed measurable serialization point in the shim.
- 21:40 - experiment A: reduced slot reclamation batch size from 32 -> 16 in the shim (non-persistent change). Immediate improvement: median unchanged, 95th reduced ~18ms in sandbox.
- 21:55 - experiment B: disabled a newly-introduced prefill coalescer heuristic (temporal threshold) for one host in staging; production shadowing suggested similar 95th improvement without throughput regressions.
- 22:15 - rolled a lightweight hotfix to one canary (10% traffic) toggling reclamation size and disabling heuristic together. Monitored for 30 minutes; no error increase, visible tail reduction for that canary group.

Observed signals
- 95th latency: canary group dropped by ~15-20ms; other groups unchanged.
- Token throughput: no material drop in the canary; CPU on the host rose by ~3% (expected due to more frequent reclamation calls).
- Error rate: unchanged.
- Queue depth histogram: fewer long-lived entries in the canary; shape suggests fewer requests stuck waiting for slot reassign.

Decisions made (temporary, tonight)
- Keep the canary enabled for an additional 24 hours to gather more traffic patterns across different regions.
- Rollback plan: if error rate > +0.5% or 95th latency fails to improve after 60 minutes at steady traffic, revert canary toggle via the rollout console. Riley to own rollback.
- No permanent config change until we have thorough perf runs and a short A/B on Dedicated workloads.

Action items and owners (next 72 hours)
- Liam: prepare a small patch that paramaterizes slot-reclamation size and exposes a runtime flag (SERVE-4821). Add microbench results for reclamation sizes 8/16/32 and a note on CPU cost. Due: 2029-06-21.
- Chen: run an expanded sandbox matrix with sequence-length distributions drawn from last 7 days (short/long/mixed). Produce a short report with heatmaps and the newly-defined "burst tail-ratio" metric. Due: 2029-06-20.
- Diego: audit prefilling coalescer heuristics; enumerate which heuristics are safe to disable early during bursts and which require a graceful fallback. Document in Confluence. Due: 2029-06-22.
- Riley: keep the canary under observation, run hourly checks for the next 24 hours, and escalate if any of the rollback criteria hit. Post a short status in #serve-ops every 3 hours. Due: ongoing 2029-06-19.
- Asha: consolidate tonight's logs/traces into the incident bucket and tag with burst-2029-06-18; coordinate a follow-up triage meeting Mon 2029-06-24 (invite kernel, kv-cache, and SRE).

Notes for engineering follow-up
- The microkernel shim appears to be a serialization point when eviction and reclamation calls interleave. We should consider if the shim needs a small per-core queue to decouple the eviction path from the slot-granting path.
- We introduced "burst tail-ratio" as a quick metric: fraction of requests whose enqueue->start time exceeds median by >X ms during a 3-minute window. Chen will define X and baseline thresholds. This metric may be helpful for future canaries.
- Consider adding a short-circuit: when the coalescer detects a rapid increase in short requests, prefer reclamation-size=16 and temporarily disable the temporal coalescer heuristic until the burst subsides.

Risks and open questions
- Small increase in CPU due to more frequent reclamation; acceptable for canary hosts but may matter at fleet scale. Need cost vs latency tradeoff analysis.
- Is there any long-tail interaction with quantized kernels or mobile-optimized model variants? (Chen to test.)
- Do we need an observability tweak: currently the enqueue->start time has 10ms resolution in some hosts; tighten to 1ms for precise burst work.

Appendix: quick commands and results (cheat-sheet)
- Toggle canary via Rollouts: console.redwood/internal/rollouts/serve-canary -> set reclaim_size=16 and coalescer_flag=false.
- Profile command: ./tools/replay --trace burst-2029-06-18 --seed-sampler mixed --out heatmap.json
- Quick grep for shim queue waits: rg "shim.*reclaim.*wait_ms" /var/log/serve/* | tail -n 200

Sign-off
Asha Patel (ops lead)
Liam O'Connor (kernel)
Chen Li (profiling)
Riley Morgan (oncall)
Diego Alvarez (kv-cache)

If you are taking daytime ownership, please read the action items and confirm on the thread. This doc is intentionally terse — save the long writeup for the Mon triage if needed.
